content:
Label the coins in the triangular arrangement as

\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
&&A\\
&B&&C\\
D&&E&&F
\end{array}
\]

Take each coin to have radius \(1\), so adjacent coin centers are \(2\) units apart.

### A construction using two moves
Keep coins \(A,C,D,E\) fixed. Move:

- coin \(B\) to the new upper-left position;
- coin \(F\) to the new leftmost position.

The resulting arrangement has centers in the pattern

\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
&&\text{new}&&A\\
\text{new}&&&&C\\
&D&&E
\end{array}
\]

which is a regular hexagon of side length \(2\). Thus the six coins form the required circle, so two moves suffice.

### Why one move is impossible
If only one coin were moved, five coins would remain in their original positions. Any five of the original six positions contain three collinear centers:

- \(D,E,F\) are collinear;
- \(A,B,D\) are collinear;
- \(A,C,F\) are collinear.

Removing any one coin leaves at least one of these triples intact. However, the six centers in the final circular arrangement are vertices of a regular hexagon, and no three vertices of a regular hexagon are collinear. Hence one move cannot work.

Therefore, the smallest number of coins that must be moved is

\[
\boxed{2}
\]
